fact: A goroutine starts with a small stack of at least 2 KiB (stackMin = 2048 on Linux/amd64) that grows on demand.
The Go runtime, not the OS, creates goroutines: newproc1 reuses a dead G from gfget or allocates one with malg(stackMin) and makes it runnable.
The runtime can preempt a goroutine in the middle of a loop by signalling its thread (asynchronous preemption).
GOMAXPROCS limits how many OS threads execute user Go code at once; it is not the number of goroutines or threads.
A reused goroutine may start with a larger stack sized from the average stack use the GC observed, never below fixedStack.
Each goroutine has a runtime descriptor, the struct runtime.g.
The runtime numbers goroutines internally in g.goid; no public API exposes the number.
Stack traces print the internal number as "goroutine N".
A go statement evaluates the function value and arguments in the calling goroutine, runs the call in a new goroutine and returns nothing (spec section id, not a Go declaration).
go f(x) evaluates f and x in the calling goroutine and runs the call in a new goroutine (spec section id, not a Go declaration).
newproc runs on the system stack, creates the G with newproc1, queues it with runqput(pp, newg, true) and then calls wakep once mainStarted.
A newly allocated G gets the minimum stack, 2 KiB on Linux.
newproc1 takes a dead G from gfget or creates one with malg(stackMin).
A reused G whose stack is not startingStackSize gets it freed and a new startingStackSize stack allocated, so reuse does not promise zero allocations.
The starting size for reused Gs is recomputed at each GC from average scanned stack usage, unless GODEBUG adaptivestackstart=0.
GODEBUG adaptivestackstart is on by default (debug.adaptivestackstart = 1).
differs: symbol renamed only: in 1.24.7 the default is set in parsedebugvars, in 1.26.1+ in parseRuntimeDebugVars; default 1 in all three

fact: newproc1 sets newg.sched.sp and newg.sched.pc = goexit + PCQuantum before calling gostartcallfn.
On amd64, gostartcall pushes the saved PC (goexit) onto the new stack as the return address and stores fn in sched.pc and the closure in sched.ctxt.
runqput(pp, gp, true) prefers runnext but uses the ordinary queue without sysmon or, randomly, under -race.
After queuing, newproc calls wakep so an idle P can start and steal the new G.
The runtime has internal goroutine IDs (g.goid) but exposes no public current-ID API.
stackalloc serves small stacks from the per-P mcache.stackcache or stackpool free lists and larger ones from stackLarge or a dedicated span, never through mallocgc.
Stack spans are manually managed spans from allocManual, not swept GC heap objects and not counted in heapInUse.
A growing stack is copied to a new, larger allocation, so its address changes.
MemStats.StackInuse is bytes in stack spans, not bytes used by live frames.
The per-P free-stack cache lives in mcache.stackcache, one list per size order.
g.sched.sp is the saved resume stack pointer.
g.stack.lo and g.stack.hi bound the allocated stack region.
Unused stack spans are returned to the heap at the end of GC.
StackSys is StackInuse plus OS-thread stack memory obtained directly from the OS, and does not count every C stack.
When the prologue's stack check fails, morestack calls newstack, which allocates a stack at least twice the old size and copies the frames.
copystack fixes pointers into the old stack using the compiler's stack pointer maps.
Escape analysis keeps pointers to stack objects out of the heap, so user heap objects never point into a stack.
runtime.main sets maxstacksize to 1000000000 bytes on 64-bit systems and 250000000 on 32-bit systems.
Growth beyond maxstacksize prints "goroutine stack exceeds N-byte limit" and throws "stack overflow".
Exceeding the stack limit is a fatal throw that cannot be recovered.
On amd64, small frameless leaf functions and NOSPLIT functions get no stack-split check in the prologue.
When stackguard0 == stackPreempt, newstack handles a preemption request instead of growing the stack.
newstack starts with twice the old size and doubles again until funcMaxSPDelta + stackGuard fits.
When a G has active channel references, copystack locks the channels and adjusts sudog pointers into the stack.
shrinkstack halves the stack only if usage (hi - sp + stackNosplit) is below a quarter, the half is at least fixedStack and isShrinkStackSafe allows it.
The GC shrinks stacks while scanning them, or defers it to a synchronous safe point through preemptShrink.
The default per-goroutine limit is 1 GB on 64-bit and 250 MB on 32-bit systems.
Stack sizes are powers of two, so the largest stack under the 1000000000-byte default is 2^29 bytes = 512 MiB.
debug.SetMaxStack sets the per-goroutine limit for future growth, returns the previous value, and exceeding it crashes the program.
A uintptr is an integer, not a pointer the GC tracks or adjusts when a stack moves.
On amd64 the current G is in R14 under ABIInternal.
gogo stores the G in TLS and R14, restores SP, BP and the closure context, clears those gobuf fields and jumps to the saved PC (assembly TEXT symbol).
differs: 1.24.7: gogo also loads gobuf.ret into AX and clears it; gobuf.ret was removed in Go 1.25, so 1.26.1/1.27.3 restore only SP, ctxt, BP and PC

fact: mcall saves the caller's PC, SP and BP in g.sched, switches R14 and SP to g0 and calls the scheduler function there (assembly TEXT symbol).
Each M has a g0 whose stack is the thread's system stack.
On g0 the scheduler calls execute, which marks the G running and calls gogo(&gp.sched).
g.sched is a gobuf holding sp, pc, g, ctxt, lr and bp: continuation state, not every CPU register.
differs: 1.24.7: gobuf also has a ret field (removed in Go 1.25); 1.26.1 and 1.27.3: sp, pc, g, ctxt, lr, bp

fact: On amd64, gogo restores SP, BP and the closure context, clears selected gobuf fields and jumps to the saved PC (assembly TEXT symbol).
differs: 1.24.7: gogo also loads gobuf.ret into AX and clears it; gobuf.ret was removed in Go 1.25, so 1.26.1/1.27.3 restore only SP, ctxt, BP and PC

symbol: Function call argument and result passing
fact: Go's internal ABI has no callee-save registers, so a voluntary switch at a call needs only the continuation state (Markdown section, not a Go declaration).
Asynchronous preemption first saves every register on the goroutine's stack (assembly TEXT symbol).
differs: 1.24.7: asyncPreempt saves flags, GP registers and X0-X15 on the goroutine stack (ADJSP $368); 1.26.1+ (since Go 1.26): only flags and GP registers go on the stack (ADJSP $112), vector registers go to p.xRegs.scratch and xRegSave moves them to off-stack gp.xRegs.state

fact: On amd64, arm64 and loong64, asynchronous preemption saves the vector registers outside the goroutine stack, in per-G state gp.xRegs.state.
differs: absent in 1.24.7: file added in Go 1.26 (also absent in the 1.25.1 tree); before that the vector registers were saved on the goroutine stack

fact: On arm64 the current G is in R28.
G1 evaluates the function value and arguments of go doWork(n); the new goroutine runs the call (spec section id, not a Go declaration).
runnext is a single slot: a new G from go takes it, and the previous occupant moves to the tail of the local runq.
systemstack switches R14 and SP to g0 while m.curg still points to the user G (assembly TEXT symbol).
G2 comes from the free pool (gfget) or is newly allocated (malg).
A new G gets 2 KiB on Linux/amd64; a pooled G gets the adaptive starting size, never below 2 KiB.
For go doWork(n) the compiler evaluates n in the caller and wraps the call in a generated closure (main.main.gowrap1) that holds the copy.
On amd64, goexit is pushed as the wrapper's return address; sched.pc becomes the wrapper entry and sched.ctxt the closure.
Without sysmon (wasm) runnext is not used; under -race the runtime puts the G in the ordinary queue with probability 1/2.
execute moves the G from runnable to running and calls gogo.
gogo restores the current G, SP, BP and closure context, then jumps to the saved PC (assembly TEXT symbol).
differs: 1.24.7: gogo also loads gobuf.ret into AX and clears it; gobuf.ret was removed in Go 1.25, so 1.26.1/1.27.3 restore only SP, ctxt, BP and PC

fact: schedtick is incremented only when the time slice is not inherited.
After the function returns, goexit calls goexit1, which calls mcall(goexit0) to switch to g0.
goexit0 calls gdestroy, which sets _Gdead and calls gfput, and then calls schedule.
gfput puts the dead G into the free pool and frees its stack if it is not startingStackSize.
On overflow the runtime prints "goroutine stack exceeds 1000000000-byte limit" and throws "stack overflow"; growth at least doubles the stack.
The GC can shrink an underused stack.
Per-iteration loop variables apply when the file's Go version is at least go1.22; older language versions share one variable.
A module declaring go 1.25 or go 1.26 needs a toolchain at least that new; with GOTOOLCHAIN=local, Go 1.24.7 refuses to build it.
differs: 1.24.7 cannot build a module that declares go 1.25 or 1.26 (go.mod requires go >= 1.25); with go 1.22-1.24 in go.mod it prints the same 0, 1, 2

fact: Since Go 1.22 each iteration of a for clause has its own variable; before, iterations shared one (spec section id, not a Go declaration).
Closing a channel is synchronized before a receive that returns because the channel is closed (memory model section id, not a Go declaration).
WaitGroup.Wait blocks until the counter reaches zero; it ensures completion, not order.
Wait blocks until every Done; a sender blocked on a full buffer never calls Done, so reading only after Wait hangs.
WaitGroup.Go(func()) exists from Go 1.25 (api/go1.25.txt); the example uses only Add, Done and Wait, which exist from Go 1.0.
differs: WaitGroup.Go is absent in 1.24.7 and present in 1.26.1 and 1.27.3, whose docs recommend it over Add/Done; Add, Done and Wait are in all three

fact: A send on a full buffered channel blocks until a receiver frees a slot.
close does not wait for the buffer to drain; receives return the remaining values, then zero values (spec section id, not a Go declaration).
